title: Reading the Floor
passage:
At half past six the indoor school is lit, empty and cold, and the tractor is already in it, towing a leveller down the long side. What it is levelling is not soil. The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand, mixed through with chopped fibre and coated in wax, laid over a membrane and crushed stone. It went down nine years ago. For two winters the riders here have been saying that the school changes under them: hard and slippery for a January lesson, deep and tiring by a July afternoon. The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor.

Mervyn Pallenmoor tests riding surfaces for an insurer that covers about four hundred livery yards. He came in February with a cone penetrometer in the boot: a steel cone on a rod, under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall. It gives two figures – how deep the cone sinks on the first blow, and how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres. A maximum-minimum thermometer hung by the gate overnight. He read a grid of thirty points at seven, with the school at three degrees, and the same grid at four, with it at eighteen. Both figures moved, and they moved together: in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled. He has been back four times since, in July as well as January. He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas, some of them older than this one. In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move, whatever their age. “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is,” Pallenmoor says. “I can’t put a number on it; these readings won’t carry one, and the blend on the grains changes from one supplier to the next. The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.”

The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work. Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface. Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep. Then there is the machine, though not in the way the yard had blamed it. The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130. Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on. Pallenmoor cored the bed in eleven places. In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3. Harrowing lifts fibre, and fibre keeps sand from packing, so the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one. The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.

The yard wants to know whether any of this keeps a horse sound. Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him. The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone. He has readings from a hundred and forty arenas and injury records he would trust from hardly any of them: the yards with good records do everything else well. The one association he will argue for is not with any surface but with change – a horse schooled on one footing and jumped on another – and he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures. That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.

The yard has changed one thing and left the other alone. The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres, with a length of angle iron welded across the frame so that nobody has to set them by eye, and for a month the tractor went over twice a day to bring the pan up. Heaters have been costed and not ordered: the quote came to more than a month of winter lessons. Pallenmoor is booked in again for the second Tuesday in March. At ten past seven the tine marks run the length of the school in even rows, the first riders are at the gate, and the thermometer beside them reads four.
– Bridget Tullis

questions.rationale:
C is right. The same cone, dropped the same way, behaved differently at the two temperatures: “in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled”. The two figures moved in opposite arithmetic directions, one down and one up, and both of them say the floor was harder in the cold.

A drives the cone further than the method does. What is counted is “how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres”, a fixed mark thirty short of the “130 millimetres” the floor is built to, so the bottom of the bed is not where a reading stops.

B offers a reason for the cold figures that the method rules out. The weight is “raised to a collar and let fall”, which is the one thing a drop test cannot be allowed to vary; a reader who wants the difference explained away as sloppy work will reach for this.

D turns the comparison in the quotation the other way up. What Pallenmoor says is that “The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test”: the seasons separate his readings by more than the arenas do, not by less.

questions.prompt: What did Pallenmoor find when he sampled the bed?

options.text: The wax had worn off the grains in the lower part of the bed.
The sand had broken down into finer grains than the specification called for.
Below the tines the bed had stayed loose, out of reach of the hoofprints above it.
There was much less fibre in the bottom of the bed than in the top.

questions.rationale:
D is right. Pallenmoor “cored the bed in eleven places”, and the cores divide it in two: “In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3.” The fibre sits where the tines reach and thins out below them.

A moves a real finding to the wrong end of the bed. The wax was looked at, and what came up was the opposite: “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top”.

B is the ageing story that a nine-year-old floor invites, and the sieve refuses it: “the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them”.

C reads like the sensible consequence of a machine that stops short of the bottom, and the passage says the reverse twice in one sentence. The layer the tines miss “had gone firm enough to lean a spade on”, and it was “under nine years of hoofprints” that it got that way, so the load of those hoofprints reaches it after all.

questions.prompt: What is suggested about schools that are kept damp with a sprinkler?

options.text: They went down more recently, so their sand has not had nine years of hooves on it.
Having no wax on their sand is what leaves them riding much the same all day.
A membrane under them holds the water in and keeps the bed from drying through the day.
They are read at a different hour, so the change falls between his two grids.

questions.rationale:
B is right. Two things are true of the damp schools at once: they carry no wax on their sand, and a sprinkler keeps them damp. The contrast runs on the coating and not on the water. Their two grids “sit almost on top of one another”, while “The waxed ones move, whatever their age”. Take the coating away and the hour of the day stops mattering.

A reaches for age, which the passage has already closed off. The other arenas are a mixed set – “some of them older than this one” – and the waxed floors swing whatever age they are.

C builds the damp schools a membrane out of this school’s own foundations. The only membrane the piece names lies under the school being tested, which is “laid over a membrane and crushed stone”, and that school is on the moving side of the contrast, not the steady one. The passage gives the other schools a different reason for staying damp: they are “kept damp with a sprinkler”, so the water is put on from above, not held in below. What marks them off is the bed itself, “laid on plain sand and fibre”.

D would explain the flat readings away as an artefact of timing. It cannot: he has “the same pair of grids” from every arena, “the morning grid and the afternoon grid” alike.

questions.prompt: What position does the writer take in this piece?

options.text: She takes the limits he sets on his own figures to be his real contribution.
She reads what the yard has since done as an answer to the soundness question.
She treats the riders’ account as the thing the readings were brought in to correct.
She rates the trade’s brochures the fuller answer to the question the yard is asking.

questions.rationale:
A is right. The writer gives her verdict in the paragraph itself. Pallenmoor “is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him”, and what he does claim “is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are”. She backs the limit, not the promise.

B reads the yard’s decision as a verdict on soundness, which is the one thing the paragraph puts out of reach: “The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone.” What was changed was how the floor rides, not what the floor does to a horse. He has “readings from a hundred and forty arenas and injury records he would trust from hardly any of them”, so the evidence that might have joined the two is exactly what he trusts least.

C points the correction at the riders. Their account is the one claim the readings bear out – “Both figures moved, and they moved together” – and it is the yard’s own explanations, “the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor”, that the piece corrects.

D keeps the fuller offer and drops the ranking that the same sentence gives it. The brochures do offer more than he will, and that is the writer’s point against them: what he says “is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are”.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this text?

options.text: In the cold the grains are probably freezing to one another in a school with no heating.
A school that is kept warm will ride in February much as it rides in July.
How the floor rides turns on the room’s temperature and the depth of the tines.
The tractor’s work may matter more to the school than the temperature does.

questions.rationale:
C is right. Two things are shown to govern the floor: the temperature, which Pallenmoor says is “doing more in that room than the tractor is”, and the depth of the tines, which had been leaving eighty millimetres of the bed unturned since the day it went down. The yard has since dropped the tines and left the temperature alone, which changes what the floor does on a given morning but not what governs it.

A gives the cold the wrong mechanism. The passage has the coating stiffening below six degrees, so that “the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface”, and it names the wax as the thing “doing most of that work”. The morning grid was read “with the school at three degrees”, which is cold and still above freezing: a stiffened coating locks the grains, not ice.

B treats the wax as if it had one threshold, and it has two. Heating a school in February lifts the room clear of the stiff end of the range, below about six degrees, but heat of that order does not take a room past twenty-five, and it is above about twenty-five that the coating “goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep”. The July afternoon sits in that upper range; a warmed February morning sits between the two marks, and a floor between them rides like neither.

D reverses the weight the passage puts on the two. The sentence is a plain one: “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is”. The tractor’s work counts, but it counts for less.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: The physical claims are the ordinary behaviour of a waxed sand-and-fibre arena surface and are stated at the level the passage can support. Wax-coated silica sand with chopped synthetic fibre stiffens as the coating hardens in cold and loosens as it softens in heat; a watered, unwaxed sand-and-fibre bed does not have that coating and so does not swing with the room's temperature in the same way. Harrowing lifts fibre towards the top of the bed, and the layer below the tines consolidates under repeated hoof loading, which is why a shallow tine setting produces a loose layer riding on a firm one. The instrument is a drop-weight cone penetrometer, described only by what it does - a steel cone on a rod, a ring weight raised to a collar and dropped, a depth on the first blow and a blow count to a fixed 100 mm - which is how such a device is used on a sports surface; a stiffer bed takes a shallower first blow and a higher count, which is the direction the passage states. Temperature is taken with a maximum-minimum thermometer, an ordinary piece of yard equipment. Results are given as relative differences (two-thirds as deep, the count nearly doubled) rather than as absolute figures, so no numerical claim is made that a specialist could check against a particular instrument. The temperatures are given as approximate ranges with 'about'. Nothing in the unit names a real product, blend, manufacturer or standard.

edits.to: B treats the wax as if it had one threshold, and it has two. The July afternoon sits in that upper range; a warmed February morning sits between the two marks, and a floor between them rides like neither.
